facts.statehood_note: Maine was part of Massachusetts (called the District of Maine) until 1820. Voters approved separating in July 1819, and Maine was admitted as the 23rd state, a free state, under the Missouri Compromise of 1820.
facts.name_origin: No one knows for certain. The name was officially recorded in 1622 (sometimes spelled 'Mayne'). Ideas include a French province, an English village, or a sailors' word for 'mainland.' A 2001 resolution of the Maine Legislature named the French province of Maine, but historians do not agree. Maine is the only state with a one-syllable name.

government.chambers: Maine Senate (35 members) and Maine House of Representatives (151 members); members of both serve two-year terms, with a limit of four terms in a row. The House also has seats for three non-voting members who represent the Penobscot Nation, the Passamaquoddy Tribe, and the Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians.
government.executive: Governor (elected every four years; no one may serve more than two terms in a row). The governor leads the Executive Branch, which carries out the laws the Legislature makes.
government.courts: The Maine Constitution puts the state's judicial power in the Supreme Judicial Court, Maine's highest court, which has seven justices: a chief justice and six associate justices. Other courts include the Superior Court and District Court. Judges are appointed by the governor, confirmed by the state Senate, and serve seven-year terms.
government.local: 16 counties, along with city and town governments.
government.constitution: Current constitution written at a convention that opened in Portland on October 11, 1819; all 210 delegates approved it, and Maine voters approved it in December 1819, just before statehood.
government.kid_line: "All people are born equally free and independent, and have certain natural, inherent and unalienable rights" (Maine Constitution, Article I, Section 1).

long_ago.about: The Penobscot live along the Penobscot River; their name refers to 'the place of the white rocks.' For nearly 1,000 years, Penobscot ancestors harvested oysters each winter and early spring on the Damariscotta River, leaving a shell heap more than 30 feet high.
Passamaquoddy ancestors lived for thousands of years around the St. Croix River and the Bay of Fundy. The Passamaquoddy name means 'people of the pollock-spearing place.'

Many Maliseet call themselves Wolastoqiyik, 'people of the Saint John River.' Like other Wabanaki peoples, they traveled the rivers by birchbark canoe, sewn with spruce root over a cedar frame and sealed with spruce gum.

The Mi'kmaq are one of the Wabanaki, the 'People of the Dawnland,' whose homeland stretches from Quebec and the Canadian Maritimes into Vermont. Mi'kmaq artists are known for delicate boxes decorated with porcupine quills.
The Abenaki are also Wabanaki people. Wabanaki families moved with the seasons, from the coast inland, fishing, hunting, gathering wild blueberries, and making baskets from brown ash and sweetgrass.

today.about: A federally recognized nation with its tribal headquarters on Indian Island in the Penobscot River near Old Town.
A federally recognized tribe with two reservations in Washington County: Motahkomikuk (Indian Township) and Sipayik (Pleasant Point).
Federally recognized in 1980, with a tribal center on its lands along the Meduxnekeag River near Houlton.
Federally recognized in 1991 (formerly called the Aroostook Band of Micmacs).

first_peoples.today_note: Maine has four federally recognized tribes, together called the Wabanaki Nations: the Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians, the Mi'kmaq Nation, the Passamaquoddy Tribe, and the Penobscot Nation. Under the Maine Indian Claims Settlement Act of 1980, the Passamaquoddy, Penobscot, and Maliseet gave up their legal land claims and received about $81 million to buy back about 300,000 acres of homeland; the act also left the state with power over many tribal matters.
sites: Abbe Museum, near Acadia National Park, which holds the largest and best documented collection of Maine Indian basketry
Penobscot Nation Museum on Indian Island, a tribal museum telling Penobscot history in the nation's own words
Waponahki Museum at Sipayik (Pleasant Point), a Passamaquoddy tribal museum
Whaleback Shell Midden State Historic Site on the Damariscotta River, part of one of North America's largest shell middens

history.event: After the glaciers melt back, Indigenous peoples begin living in the land now called Maine. Wabanaki stories say they have always been here.

French explorers, including Samuel de Champlain, build a settlement on Saint Croix Island. In the hard winter 35 of the 79 men die; Passamaquoddy people bring supplies in March 1605, and the French leave that June.
About 100 English colonists led by George Popham build a fort near the mouth of the Kennebec River. The Popham Colony fails within a year, but the settlers build the Virginia, a small ship.
During King Philip's War, Wabanaki nations form the Wabanaki Confederacy and aid the Wampanoag and Mahican. Wars between Wabanaki peoples and English colonists go on for decades.

Penobscot leader Joseph Orono goes to the Massachusetts Provincial Congress and offers support to the American side if Penobscot complaints, such as trespass and unfair trade, are fixed. The Penobscots support the Americans through the Revolution.
Through treaties and other deals, millions of acres of Wabanaki land pass to Massachusetts, then Maine, and to private owners.
In the War of 1812, British troops occupy the eastern third of Maine. Massachusetts sends little help, which pushes many people in Maine to want their own state.
In July, voters approve separating from Massachusetts. A convention opens in Portland on October 11 to write a constitution, and voters approve it in December.
Maine becomes the 23rd state, entering as a free state under the Missouri Compromise. William King is elected the first governor.
Black members of a Portland church, made to sit in separate seats, form their own congregation and build the Abyssinian Meeting House, a church, school, and center for anti-slavery work.
In the 'bloodless' Aroostook War, Maine and New Brunswick argue over the border with no battles. The Webster–Ashburton Treaty of 1842 settles the line.
In Brunswick, Harriet Beecher Stowe writes Uncle Tom's Cabin, a novel against slavery published as a book in 1852.
Maine sends more than 70,000 men to the Union army. On July 2, 1863, at Gettysburg, the 20th Maine under Joshua Chamberlain holds Little Round Top at the far left of the Union line.

During Reconstruction, Maine general Oliver Otis Howard leads the Freedmen's Bureau, which helped people freed from slavery, and founds Howard University. Joshua Chamberlain serves as governor from 1867 to 1871.

trailblazers.name: Joseph Orono
trailblazers.text: Joseph Orono led the Penobscot Nation from 1760 until his death in 1801. In 1775 he traveled to the Massachusetts Provincial Congress to offer Penobscot support for the American cause if the nation's complaints about trespass and unfair trade were fixed. The town of Orono, Maine, carries his name.

trailblazers.name: Reuben Ruby
trailblazers.text: Reuben Ruby was born in Gray, Maine, in 1798 and became a leader of Portland's Black community. In 1834 he helped found the Maine Anti-Slavery Society, and in 1835 he was elected president of a national convention for the rights of free Black Americans in Philadelphia.

trailblazers.name: Macon Bolling Allen
trailblazers.text: After first being turned away, Macon Bolling Allen earned his license to practice law in Maine on July 3, 1844, after training in Portland; he is known as the first African American attorney in the United States. He later became a justice of the peace in Massachusetts and a judge in Charleston, South Carolina, during Reconstruction.

trailblazers.name: Harriet Beecher Stowe
trailblazers.text: Harriet Beecher Stowe moved to Brunswick in 1850 when her husband took a teaching job at Bowdoin College. There she began writing Uncle Tom's Cabin, an anti-slavery novel that sold ten thousand copies in its first week in 1852.

trailblazers.name: Louis Sockalexis
trailblazers.text: Louis Sockalexis was born on Indian Island, Penobscot Nation, and went to the College of the Holy Cross. In 1897 he joined the Cleveland Spiders and became the first widely recognized Native American major league baseball player, even though crowds mocked him with racist taunts.

trailblazers.name: Margaret Chase Smith
trailblazers.text: Margaret Chase Smith of Skowhegan was the first woman to serve in both the U.S. House and the U.S. Senate, and the first woman to represent Maine in either. On June 1, 1950, her 'Declaration of Conscience' speech defended Americans' rights to criticize, to hold unpopular beliefs, and to protest, and in 1964 she became the first woman to actively seek the presidential nomination of a major political party.

trailblazers.name: Toy Len Goon
trailblazers.text: Toy Len Goon arrived in Portland from China in 1921, speaking no English. After her husband died in 1941, she ran the family laundry and raised eight children, making sure all of them got a good education. In 1952 she was named American Mother of the Year.

landforms: Mount Katahdin (5,269 feet), the tallest mountain in Maine; its Penobscot name means 'The Greatest Mountain'
Cadillac Mountain and the pink granite cliffs of Acadia National Park on Mount Desert Island
A rocky coastline about 3,500 miles long with many islands
Wild blueberry barrens on rocky soils left by glaciers
waters: Gulf of Maine (about 36,000 square miles of the North Atlantic)
More than 6,000 lakes and ponds and 31,000 miles of rivers and streams
geography.regions: Maine has a jagged, rocky Atlantic coast, mountains in the interior and west, a huge North Woods forest dotted with lakes and rivers, and farmland in Aroostook County in the far north.

ecosystems.name: Gulf of Maine
ecosystems.about: A nearly enclosed sea that is home to 32 kinds of marine mammals, including about 1,700 humpback whales that spend much of their time there. Its waters are warming fast, and cod and lobster are moving north toward cooler seas.

ecosystems.name: North Woods forest
ecosystems.about: Maine's moose population is about 60,000 to 70,000, the highest in the lower 48 states. Lynx, bear, and deer also live in the woods around Katahdin.

ecosystems.name: Wild blueberry barrens
ecosystems.about: Glaciers scraped the land about 10,000 years ago, leaving rocky, acidic soil where wild blueberries grow. Wabanaki people picked them for food, medicine, and dye and used controlled fires to help new plants grow.

ecosystems.name: Salmon rivers
ecosystems.about: Young Atlantic salmon swim from Maine rivers all the way to the waters off Newfoundland and Labrador, then return years later to lay eggs. The Gulf of Maine salmon were listed as endangered in 2000, and dam removals are helping them come back.

science.weather: Maine has warm summers and long, cold, very snowy winters, harshest in the north and west. Nor'easters bring heavy storms to the coast in late fall and winter.
science.resources: Forests cover most of Maine and supply paper, lumber, and wood products. Maine is the top U.S. producer of lobster and wild blueberries, grows potatoes in Aroostook County, and also makes maple syrup and welcomes many tourists.
science.highlight: Whales of the Gulf of Maine: humpback whales in the North Atlantic dropped to about 2,000 by 1986, when commercial whaling was banned. Today there are nearly 18,000, but North Atlantic right whales are still in danger, with fewer than 400 left.

g3_ss.title: Maine's Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Find Augusta and Portland on a map, learn the motto 'Dirigo' (I lead), and meet the Legislature's 35 senators and 151 representatives plus its three tribal seats.

g3_ss.title: The Wabanaki, People of the Dawnland
g3_ss.plan: Meet the Penobscot, Passamaquoddy, Maliseet, Mi'kmaq, and Abenaki; look at birchbark canoes and ash and sweetgrass baskets; visit the Penobscot Nation Museum online.

g3_ss.title: Maine Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Make trading cards for Joseph Orono, Reuben Ruby, Louis Sockalexis, Margaret Chase Smith, and Toy Len Goon.

g45_ss.title: Maine's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: Use the Whaleback shell midden, wild blueberry burning, and Wabanaki place names like Katahdin to learn how the Wabanaki lived with the seasons, then learn about the four Wabanaki Nations today.

g45_ss.title: Contact, Colonies, and Conflict
g45_ss.plan: Compare the Saint Croix Island winter of 1604 (with Passamaquoddy help) and the Popham Colony, then trace wars over land and Joseph Orono's choice in the Revolution.

g45_ss.title: Maine 1820–1877
g45_ss.plan: Explain statehood under the Missouri Compromise, Portland's Black community and the Abyssinian Meeting House, Macon Bolling Allen, Uncle Tom's Cabin, the 20th Maine, and Oliver Otis Howard's Freedmen's Bureau.

g3_sci.title: Moose of the North Woods
g3_sci.plan: Learn moose body parts and needs, why the herd shrank to about 2,000 and grew back to 60,000 to 70,000, and how winter ticks harm calves.

g3_sci.title: Blueberry Barrens
g3_sci.plan: Explore how glaciers made rocky soil, how wild blueberries grow, and how Wabanaki people used fire to care for the barrens.

g3_sci.title: Lobsters and the Sea
g3_sci.plan: Study a lobster's body and life in the Gulf of Maine, and why warming water moves lobsters north.

g45_sci.title: The Gulf of Maine
g45_sci.plan: Map the Gulf, study its food web and 32 marine mammals, and graph the humpback whale comeback since 1986.

g45_sci.title: Glaciers and Mount Katahdin
g45_sci.plan: Investigate how ice sheets shaped Maine's mountains, lakes, rocky coast, and soils, using Katahdin and Acadia's granite as examples.

g45_sci.title: Saving the Atlantic Salmon and the Ash Tree
g45_sci.plan: Follow the salmon life cycle from river to sea and back, study how dams block them, and learn how the emerald ash borer threatens the brown ash Wabanaki basketmakers use.
